prompt: Why does a honeypot need no tuning against false positives in normal work?

choices.text: Because it only alerts on known attack signatures
choices.why: It alerts on any touch, known or not.

choices.text: Nobody's work touches it
choices.why: Right: any touch is a finding.

choices.text: Because it runs on a separate network from everything else
choices.why: It sits among the other machines, on purpose.

choices.text: Because its alerts are summarised in a weekly report
choices.why: Its alerts are never batched.

prompt: Match each kind of bait to what a touch means.

pairs.right: somebody is trying names they found

prompt: At which stage of an intrusion is bait most useful inside a firm?

choices.text: Before anything is compromised, to keep attackers away
choices.why: Bait keeps nobody away; it notices them.

choices.text: After the first machine, when they look around
choices.why: Right: where ordinary tools in ordinary ways hide them.

choices.text: Only when data is already leaving the firm
choices.why: Honeytokens help there too, but network bait works earlier.

choices.text: During a phishing campaign, before anybody clicks
choices.why: Nothing has reached the network yet.

prompt: Why is low interaction preferred for a honeypot inside the firm?

choices.text: Because high-interaction honeypots are illegal in Brazil
choices.why: The lesson makes no such claim.

choices.text: Because it records more about each visitor
choices.why: It records less: it closes the door at once.

choices.text: There is almost nothing in it to attack
choices.why: Right: bait must never become a way in.

choices.text: Because attackers trust simple services more than complex ones
choices.why: Trust is not why.

prompt: Why does bait.py listen on 23, 445, 1433 and 3389 rather than on, say, port 47123?

choices.text: They are what somebody exploring a network tries first
choices.why: Right: bait nobody would try catches nobody.

choices.text: Because ports above 1024 cannot be logged
choices.why: Any port can be logged.

choices.text: Because Jatobá already runs those services on trap
choices.why: It runs none of them anywhere.

choices.text: Because nmap refuses to scan high ports
choices.why: nmap scans any range it is given.

prompt: Outside this lab, what should the honeypot machine be called?

choices.text: honeypot, so administrators recognise it
choices.why: An intruder would recognise it too.

choices.text: Nothing: it should have no name in DNS
choices.why: A machine with no name looks odd, and is tried less.

choices.text: Something worth a look, like sql-legacy
choices.why: Right: the name is part of the bait.

choices.text: trap, as in the lab
choices.why: The lab names it so you always know which is the bait.

prompt: The honeypot logged `touched: 192.168.60.20 on port 445`. Where does the response start?

choices.text: At desk
choices.why: Right: the machine that touched the bait.

choices.text: At trap, by checking whether it was compromised
choices.why: Nothing happened to trap; it closed the connection.

choices.text: At the firewall, by blocking port 445 everywhere
choices.why: That would hide the next touch, not explain this one.

choices.text: At web, which holds the client data
choices.why: web was not involved in this touch.

prompt: How many bait ports did the scan from desk find open on trap?
An authorised inventory scan touches the honeypot. What is the right way to handle it?

choices.text: Exclude the scanner's address in bait.py permanently
choices.why: An intruder on that machine would then be invisible.

choices.text: Switch the honeypot off during business hours
choices.why: Intruders work in business hours too.

choices.text: Know about the scan beforehand and close that alert with a note
choices.why: Right: an alert from anywhere else is not closed.

choices.text: Ignore every alert that comes from inside the firm
choices.why: Every touch the honeypot exists for comes from inside.

prompt: Why does the bait file let itself be read rather than refusing access?

choices.text: Because inotifywait only works on readable files
choices.why: It watches any file.

choices.text: A file that refused would announce it was bait
choices.why: Right: the alert comes from the opening.

choices.text: Because the credentials in it are real and needed by the backup job
choices.why: Every value in it is invented.

choices.text: Because root cannot be refused access to a file
choices.why: Root can be refused by mandatory access control, lesson 11.

prompt: Why is the svc_backup username the strongest piece of bait in the lesson?

choices.text: Because it has a long password
choices.why: The password opens nothing; length does not matter.

choices.text: Because sshd blocks it after three tries
choices.why: Blocking is fail2ban's, and is not the point here.

choices.text: Because it is stored in a hidden directory
choices.why: /srv/portal/old-backup is not hidden.

choices.text: It fires wherever the stolen file is used
choices.why: Right: not only where it was stored.

prompt: sshd logs a login attempt for an account that does not exist as `___ user svc_backup from ...`.
Why does a firm that wants to detect intrusions never put its honeypot on the internet?

choices.text: It would be touched all day by automated scans, which says nothing about the firm
choices.why: Right: noise instead of signal.

choices.text: Because honeypots are slower on public addresses
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Because a public honeypot needs a TLS certificate
choices.why: bait.py speaks no TLS; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Nobody on the internet ever scans unknown addresses
choices.why: The opposite: everybody does, constantly.

prompt: Which of these keep bait from weakening what it sits beside? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Low interaction, with nothing behind the port
choices.why: Nothing to break into.

choices.text: Credentials for an account that exists nowhere
choices.why: They open nothing.

choices.text: A real account with a weak password, disabled at night
choices.why: A way in with an alarm on it is still a way in.

choices.text: Hardening and firewalling the honeypot like any other machine
choices.why: So an attack on it leads nowhere.

prompt: How should honeypot alerts reach people?

choices.text: In a weekly summary with the other alerts
choices.why: They are never batched or summarised.

choices.text: At once, to a person, every time
choices.why: Right: they are rare by design.

choices.text: Only when three arrive within an hour
choices.why: One touch is already a finding.

choices.text: Only to the firm's internet provider
choices.why: The provider is not who responds.

prompt: What is the trade in using a service such as Canarytokens?

choices.text: It works only inside the firm's network
choices.why: Its tokens alert wherever they are used.

choices.text: Trusting a third party with the alerts
choices.why: Right: a decision like any external service.

choices.text: It needs a honeypot machine for every token
choices.why: Tokens need no machine of the firm's.

choices.text: It only covers Windows machines
choices.why: Its tokens include URLs, DNS names and cloud keys.

prompt: A honey account sits in Active Directory. What produces the alert?

choices.text: The account's password expiring
choices.why: Expiry is routine and says nothing about anybody.

choices.text: An antivirus scan of the domain controller
choices.why: The account is not a file.

choices.text: Any attempt to log in as it or request tickets for it
choices.why: Right: it appears in the domain controllers' security log.

choices.text: Its group membership being read by an administrator
choices.why: Administrators read directories all day.

prompt: Order the bait an intruder would meet, from the first move on the network to using stolen data.
items: the bait ports on trap, while scanning
the credentials file on web, while looking through files
the svc_backup login, while trying what they found

prompt: A year passes and the honeypot never fires. What is the right reading?
hint: What else would make it silent?

choices.text: The firm is safe and the honeypot can be removed
choices.why: Silence also comes from a broken honeypot.

choices.text: Test it on purpose, then keep it
choices.why: Right: a deliberate touch proves the alert still arrives.

choices.text: Expose it to the internet to get some alerts
choices.why: That brings noise, not knowledge.

choices.text: Make it interactive, so attackers stay longer
choices.why: That makes it attackable without making it more likely to fire.

prompt: A piece of data that nothing legitimate ever reads, kept to detect whoever does, is a ___.
Why does bait.py write each touch both to a JSON file and to the system log?

choices.text: In case one disk fails
choices.why: Both live on the same disk.

choices.text: The JSON is for later study; the system log is where alerts are raised from
choices.why: Right: one record for analysis, one for the alert path.

choices.text: Because syslog cannot store addresses
choices.why: The syslog line carries the address.

choices.text: To make the honeypot look busier to visitors
choices.why: Visitors never see either record.
